verses.text: In the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came, he and all his army, against Jerusalem, and encamped against it; and they built forts against it around it.
So the city was besieged until the eleventh year of king Zedekiah.
On the ninth day of the fourth month, the famine was severe in the city, so that there was no bread for the people of the land.

Then a breach was made in the city, and all the men of war fled by night by the way of the gate between the two walls, which was by the king’s garden (now the Chaldeans were against the city around it); and the king went by the way of the Arabah.
But the Chaldean army pursued the king, and overtook him in the plains of Jericho; and all his army was scattered from him.
Then they captured the king, and carried him up to the king of Babylon to Riblah; and they passed judgment on him.
They killed Zedekiah’s sons before his eyes, then put out Zedekiah’s eyes, bound him in fetters, and carried him to Babylon.

Now in the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month, which was the nineteenth year of king Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, a servant of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.
He burned Yahweh’s house, the king’s house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, even every great house, he burned with fire.
All the army of the Chaldeans, who were with the captain of the guard, broke down the walls around Jerusalem.

Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive the residue of the people who were left in the city, and those who fell away, who fell to the king of Babylon, and the residue of the multitude.
But the captain of the guard left some of the poorest of the land to work the vineyards and fields.
The Chaldeans broke up the pillars of brass that were in Yahweh’s house and the bases and the bronze sea that were in Yahweh’s house, and carried the brass pieces to Babylon.
They took away the pots, the shovels, the snuffers, the spoons, and all the vessels of brass with which they ministered.
The captain of the guard took away the fire pans, the basins, that which was of gold, in gold, and that which was of silver, in silver.
The two pillars, the one sea, and the bases, which Solomon had made for Yahweh’s house, the brass of all these vessels was not weighed.

The height of the one pillar was eighteen cubits,  and a capital of brass was on it. The height of the capital was three cubits, with network and pomegranates on the capital around it, all of brass; and the second pillar with its network was like these.
The captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, and the three keepers of the threshold;

and out of the city he took an officer who was set over the men of war; and five men of those who saw the king’s face, who were found in the city; and the scribe, the captain of the army, who mustered the people of the land; and sixty men of the people of the land, who were found in the city.
Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard took them, and brought them to the king of Babylon to Riblah.
The king of Babylon attacked them, and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah was carried away captive out of his land.
As for the people who were left in the land of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had left, even over them he made Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, governor.

Now when all the captains of the forces, they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah governor, they came to Gedaliah to Mizpah, even Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan the son of Kareah, and Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah the son of the Maacathite, they and their men.
Gedaliah swore to them and to their men, and said to them, “Don’t be afraid because of the servants of the Chaldeans. Dwell in the land, and serve the king of Babylon, and it will be well with you.”

But in the seventh month, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, of the royal offspring  came, and ten men with him, and struck Gedaliah, so that he died, with the Jews and the Chaldeans that were with him at Mizpah.
All the people, both small and great, and the captains of the forces, arose, and came to Egypt; for they were afraid of the Chaldeans.

In the thirty-seventh year of the captivity of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, Evilmerodach king of Babylon, in the year that he began to reign, lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah out of prison;
and he spoke kindly to him, and set his throne above the throne of the kings who were with him in Babylon,
and changed his prison garments. Jehoiachin ate bread before him continually all the days of his life;
and for his allowance, there was a continual allowance given him from the king, every day a portion, all the days of his life.

footnotes.content: Nebuchadnezzar's armies surround the city like a wall. When we've turned from the Lord persistently, He lets us feel the weight of that choice—not in vengeance, but as a teacher allowing the hardest lesson. We often don't learn until we're enclosed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two years the city endured the siege. Long enough for every comfortable illusion to starve away. Sometimes the Lord grants us time to watch our pride crumble, knowing that watching is part of turning back to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Famine in the city—the land itself could not feed them. The word echoes Leviticus 26, where Moses warned it would come to this. The consequences arrive not as surprise but as covenant fulfilled, mercy's last language before discipline.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king flees at night between two walls. How like fear to seek the narrow way, the darkness, the hiding place—yet there is no escape from what we've sown. The king's garden, where all seemed ordered, becomes his prison.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The plains of Jericho—where Israel's conquest began in faith, now the place of a king's rout and scattering. Full circles turn slowly, and the echo teaches us which way we've strayed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judgment comes not on the battlefield but before the king of a foreign power. Zedekiah, who refused the prophet's counsel, now faces the sentence of a heathen ruler. There is no shelter in rebellion, only exposure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king watches his sons die, then loses his sight. A terrible symmetry—he closed his eyes to the Lord's word, and now Babylon closes them forever. Yet even here, in the darkest hour, God is not done with His purposes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nebuzaradan arrives as an instrument, a servant of the Chaldean king. The armies of a pagan empire move at the Father's permission—He uses all things, even the instruments of judgment, to turn His people back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The temple burns—Yahweh's house, the palace, the city itself. In Jeremiah's scroll and the chronicles, the Lord had warned through His servants. Fire does not lie; it speaks plainly when we have stopped listening to words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The walls fall. Jerusalem, built on a height to seem secure, is brought low. The city that trusted in stones instead of the Lord finds stones no defense. Yet walls can be rebuilt; the deeper lesson is to rebuild the heart first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people are carried away captive—not all, but most. The land empties. Captivity is the exile that teaches: we do not belong to ourselves, nor to stone and soil, but only to the Lord who permits and restores.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Some of the poorest remain to tend the vineyards and fields. Even in desolation, there is mercy—the Lord does not leave the land wholly empty, nor His people wholly without hope. The smallest seed bears fruit when tended in humility.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The temple's pillars and bronze vessels are stripped and carried to Babylon. What was meant to gather God's people in worship becomes plunder. Yet the loss of bronze does not diminish the God who dwells in hearts that turn to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pots and shovels, the humble tools of ministry—all taken. The Lord's house is stripped bare. Yet He taught us that He dwells not in temples made with hands, but in the temple of a contrite heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gold and silver vessels removed—treasures that had caught the eye and the heart. The removal speaks: value is not kept by clinging; it passes only through open hands given to the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon's great pillars and the bronze sea—the achievements of a kingdom's glory—become brass to be weighed. What a sovereign makes, another can unmake. Only what God does endures.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eighteen cubits high, ornate with pomegranates in brass—the pillars stood for strength and fruitfulness. Their height meant nothing before Babylon's axes. Grandeur crumbles when it's not rooted in faithfulness to God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seraiah the chief priest and his colleagues are singled out and taken. Even the priests, who should have been buffers of holiness, are carried away. Leadership fails when it forgets whom it serves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Officers, wise men, soldiers, and common folk—all taken together into exile. The whole order crumbles, from least to greatest. Yet in exile, the Lord does not abandon His own; He walks with them and prepares a return.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The captives are brought to Riblah before the Chaldean king. Every step toward judgment is also a step toward the end of one story and the beginning of a new chapter written by God's hand, not ours.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The leading men are put to death at Riblah. Judah is now carried away completely. The exile is total, final—or so it seems. Yet we know from later promises that exile is not abandonment, only a hard schooling in faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gedaliah is appointed governor over the poorest—a remnant. The Lord leaves a seed, however small. This is covenant mercy at work: judgment is not final; restoration is already being set in place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The remaining captains gather around the new governor. Ishmael, Johanan, and others—military men, accustomed to ruling themselves. They will test Gedaliah's authority, as we all test mercy when it arrives undeserved.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gedaliah offers reassurance: fear not, serve Babylon, and it will be well. A word of prudence and peace—yet the human heart, traumatized and suspicious, sometimes cannot hear peace when it is offered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ishmael, of royal blood, strikes down Gedaliah. Even in captivity, even with mercy offered, pride and fear can spark a desperate act. Ishmael kills the one trying to hold the peace, breaking what was being healed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fear scatters the remnant toward Egypt—the very place Jeremiah warned against. Even at the edge of restoration, doubt and dread can turn us from the Lord's intended path. Yet He follows even into Egypt.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Thirty-seven years after the captivity began, Evilmerodach lifts Jehoiachin's head from prison. A date, a name, a small grace: the Lord works in history, moving through pagan rulers, holding His purposes steady.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king's son is given a seat of honor above other captive princes. After decades in darkness, light finds him. This is not forgetting what was lost, but a tender gesture that says: you are not forgotten by the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoiachin eats before the king all his days, dressed in honor instead of prison rags. A small restoration, a daily mercy. Even captive, even broken, he is fed and clothed—God's way of saying the story is not over.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An allowance, a portion, every day—consistency in care. Readers today hear an echo in this: after the exile of our own failures and separations, the Lord gives us a daily provision and a seat at His table. We are not abandoned; we are remembered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
